pointers.sentence: Both declare `async_capable = False`, so under ASGI they run synchronously ([Sync and async in one chain](../handlers/async.md)) (`django/middleware/security.py:SecurityMiddleware.async_capable`).

`SecurityMiddleware.__init__` copies its settings into attributes, and compiles each pattern of `SECURE_REDIRECT_EXEMPT` as a regular expression (`django/middleware/security.py:SecurityMiddleware.__init__`).

The host is `SECURE_SSL_HOST` if it names one, and otherwise `HttpRequest.get_host`, which raises `DisallowedHost` for a host outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS`: in a run of the example, a plain request for evil.example got a 400 and no redirect (`django/middleware/security.py:SecurityMiddleware.process_request`).

`MiddlewareMixin.__call__` passes the redirect to the same middleware's `process_response`, so it leaves with this middleware's headers, though without Strict-Transport-Security, since the request was not secure; the middleware inside it never run (`django/middleware/__init__.py:MiddlewareMixin.__call__`).
`SecurityMiddleware.process_response` adds up to four headers, in this order (`django/middleware/security.py:SecurityMiddleware.process_response`).

The browser applies the header to the whole domain and remembers it for the seconds given; Django's documentation advises starting with a small value, an hour, as the harbour office does, and raising it once everything is served over HTTPS (`docs/ref/middleware.txt`).
The documentation's reason: a browser that guesses a file's type over its Content-Type may take an uploaded file for HTML or JavaScript (`docs/ref/middleware.txt`).
The comment gives the reason as fallback: the documentation says the browser takes the last value it understands (`docs/ref/middleware.txt`).

**Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy** comes from `SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY`; the documentation describes it as isolating the site's windows from other sites' documents, against attacks like Spectre (`docs/ref/middleware.txt`).

The other three are added with `setdefault`, the last through `HttpResponseBase.setdefault`, which hands it to `ResponseHeaders.setdefault`: a header is set only when the response lacks it (`django/http/response.py:ResponseHeaders.setdefault`).
*The two middleware's settings and their defaults (`django/conf/global_settings.py`).

X-Frame-Options says whether a browser may show the response inside a frame: `"DENY"` nowhere, `"SAMEORIGIN"` only in a page of the same site, as the class's docstring says (`django/middleware/clickjacking.py:XFrameOptionsMiddleware`).

`XFrameOptionsMiddleware.process_response` leaves the response alone if it has the header already, or if it carries an attribute `"xframe_options_exempt"` that is true (`django/middleware/clickjacking.py:XFrameOptionsMiddleware.process_response`).
Its docstring invites a subclass to override it, so that the value can depend on the request or the response (`django/middleware/clickjacking.py:XFrameOptionsMiddleware.get_xframe_options_value`).
Each makes a coroutine function as its wrapper when the view is one and an ordinary function otherwise, so an async view stays async (`django/views/decorators/clickjacking.py`).
